claim: Bitter compounds elicit an aversive response.
source: Bitter compounds elicit an aversive response.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bitter taste perception.

claim: In Drosophila, bitter-sensitive taste neurons coexpress many members of the Gr family of taste receptors.
source: In Drosophila, bitter-sensitive taste neurons coexpress many members of the Gr family of taste receptors.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis data presented in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: Ectopic or overexpression of bitter Grs increased endogenous responses or conferred novel responses.
source: Ectopic or overexpression of bitter Grs increased endogenous responses or conferred novel responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Expression of Grs suppressed many endogenous bitter responses.
source: Surprisingly, expression of Grs also suppressed many endogenous bitter responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 4, 5, and related text.

claim: Deletion of an endogenous Gr led to novel responses.
source: Conversely, deletion of an endogenous Gr led to novel responses.
evidence: This is supported by data from the Gr59c deletion experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Expression of individual Grs conferred strikingly different effects in different neurons.
source: Expression of individual Grs conferred strikingly different effects in different neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by comparative data across different sensillum types shown in Figures 3-6 and summarized in Figure 11.

claim: Bitter Grs interact, exhibiting competition, inhibition, or activation.
source: The results support a model in which bitter Grs interact, exhibiting competition, inhibition, or activation.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the experimental findings of suppression, novel responses, and context-dependent effects.

claim: Many toxins elicit a bitter taste and an aversive response that is widely conserved across phyla.
source: Many toxins elicit a bitter taste and an aversive response that is widely conserved across phyla.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bitter taste function.

claim: Many bitter compounds are synthesized by plants and deter insects from feeding on them.
source: Many bitter compounds are synthesized by plants and deter insects from feeding on them (Pontes et al., 2014; Briscoe et al., 2013; Salloum et al., 2011; Sellier et al., 2011; Freeman and Dahanukar, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Insects have evolved gustatory systems that detect bitter compounds and signal the danger of toxicity.
source: Insects in turn have evolved gustatory systems that detect these compounds and signal the danger of toxicity (Wada-Katsumata et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The principal taste organ of the Drosophila head is the labellum.
source: The principal taste organ of the Drosophila head is the labellum (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The labellum contains ~31 taste sensilla that fall into morphological classes based on length: short (S), intermediate (I), and long (L).
source: The labellum contains ~31 taste sensilla that fall into morphological classes based on length: short (S; green and blue in Figure 1), intermediate (I; purple and red), and long (L; gray in Figure 1) (Stocker, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Each sensillum has a pore at its tip through which compounds from a food source diffuse to activate gustatory receptor neurons inside.
source: Each sensillum has a pore at its tip. When a sensillum makes contact with a potential food source, compounds from the food source diffuse through the pore and activate gustatory receptor neurons inside.
evidence: This is established anatomical and functional knowledge about sensillum structure.

claim: Electrophysiological analysis of all 31 sensilla with a panel of 16 bitter compounds revealed that bitter compounds elicit different responses from different sensilla.
source: Electrophysiological analysis of all 31 sensilla with a panel of 16 bitter compounds revealed that bitter compounds elicit different responses from different sensilla (Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Four functional classes of bitter-sensitive sensilla were identified: S-a, S-b, I-a, and I-b.
source: Four functional classes of bitter-sensitive sensilla were identified, two of short length, S-a and S-b, and two of intermediate length, I-a and I-b.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research (Weiss et al., 2011) and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Each class of bitter-sensitive sensilla contains a neuron excited by bitter compounds with a distinguishable response spectrum.
source: Each class contains a neuron excited by bitter compounds, referred to as a 'bitter neuron,' with a distinguishable response spectrum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research (Weiss et al., 2011).

claim: Expression analysis of all 68 members of the Gustatory receptor (Gr) family identified four corresponding classes of bitter neurons, each expressing a distinct subset of receptors.
source: Expression analysis of all 68 members of the Gustatory receptor (Gr) family identified four corresponding classes of bitter neurons, each expressing a distinct subset of receptors (Figure 1) (Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: 29 bitter receptors are coexpressed in the bitter neuron of S-a sensilla.
source: They show extensive coexpression: 29 are coexpressed in the bitter neuron of S-a
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis data from Weiss et al., 2011.

claim: 16 bitter receptors are coexpressed in the bitter neuron of S-b sensilla.
source: 16 in S-b
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis data from Weiss et al., 2011.

claim: 6 bitter receptors are coexpressed in the bitter neuron of I-a sensilla.
source: 6 in I-a
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis data from Weiss et al., 2011.

claim: 10 bitter receptors are coexpressed in the bitter neuron of I-b sensilla.
source: 10 in I-b
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis data from Weiss et al., 2011.

claim: The legs and pharynx of the fly have gustatory function.
source: In addition to the labellum, the legs and pharynx of the fly also have gustatory function, as does the larval head (Weiss et al., 2011; Kwon et al., 2011; LeDue et al., 2015; Ling et al., 2014; Meunier et al., 2003; Oppliger et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The larval head has gustatory function.
source: In addition to the labellum, the legs and pharynx of the fly also have gustatory function, as does the larval head (Weiss et al., 2011; Kwon et al., 2011; LeDue et al., 2015; Ling et al., 2014; Meunier et al., 2003; Oppliger et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Expression analysis of Grs has been based primarily on Gr-GAL4 drivers.
source: We note that expression analysis of Grs has been based primarily on Gr-GAL4 drivers, since success in analyzing Gr expression with in situ hybridization has been extremely limited.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the approach used in the field.

claim: Gr93a is required for the behavioral and physiological response to caffeine.
source: For example, Gr93a is required for the behavioral and physiological response to caffeine; Gr8a is required for response to L-canavanine; Gr66a, Gr33a and Gr32a are broadly required for the response to several bitter tastants (Lee et al., 2009; 2010; 2012; Moon et al., 2006; Moon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gr8a is required for response to L-canavanine.
source: For example, Gr93a is required for the behavioral and physiological response to caffeine; Gr8a is required for response to L-canavanine; Gr66a, Gr33a and Gr32a are broadly required for the response to several bitter tastants (Lee et al., 2009; 2010; 2012; Moon et al., 2006; Moon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gr66a, Gr33a and Gr32a are broadly required for the response to several bitter tastants.
source: For example, Gr93a is required for the behavioral and physiological response to caffeine; Gr8a is required for response to L-canavanine; Gr66a, Gr33a and Gr32a are broadly required for the response to several bitter tastants (Lee et al., 2009; 2010; 2012; Moon et al., 2006; Moon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The roles of individual Grs in bitter response have been difficult to discern in detail because of the coexpression of bitter receptors.
source: However, the roles of individual Grs in bitter response have been difficult to discern in detail, in part because of the coexpression of bitter receptors and in part because of the difficulty of expressing bitter receptors in conventional expression systems such as cultured cells or oocytes (Liman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Bitter receptors are difficult to express in conventional expression systems such as cultured cells or oocytes.
source: However, the roles of individual Grs in bitter response have been difficult to discern in detail, in part because of the coexpression of bitter receptors and in part because of the difficulty of expressing bitter receptors in conventional expression systems such as cultured cells or oocytes (Liman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about technical challenges in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Ectopic expression of Gr22b in I-a sensilla conferred an electrophysiological response to cucurbitacin (CUC) that is not observed in either parental control line.
source: We found that ectopic expression of Gr22b conferred an electrophysiological response to cucurbitacin (CUC) that is not observed in either of the parental control lines, GAL89a-GAL4; + or +/UAS-Gr22b (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2.

claim: CUC is a plant-derived compound that has insecticidal activity and tastes bitter to humans.
source: CUC is a plant-derived compound that has insecticidal activity and tastes bitter to humans (Torkey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Expression of Gr22b conferred strong responses to sucrose octaacetate (SOA) in I-a sensilla.
source: Expression of Gr22b also conferred strong responses to sucrose octaacetate (SOA), another bitter-tasting compound (Harwood et al., 2012), and to azadirachtin (AZA), which is found in the seeds of the neem tree and which inhibits feeding of locusts and many other insects (Table 1) (Schmutterer, 1990; Sharma et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: SOA is a bitter-tasting compound.
source: Expression of Gr22b also conferred strong responses to sucrose octaacetate (SOA), another bitter-tasting compound (Harwood et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Expression of Gr22b conferred strong responses to azadirachtin (AZA) in I-a sensilla.
source: Expression of Gr22b also conferred strong responses to sucrose octaacetate (SOA), another bitter-tasting compound (Harwood et al., 2012), and to azadirachtin (AZA), which is found in the seeds of the neem tree and which inhibits feeding of locusts and many other insects (Table 1) (Schmutterer, 1990; Sharma et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Azadirachtin is found in the seeds of the neem tree and inhibits feeding of locusts and many other insects.
source: and to azadirachtin (AZA), which is found in the seeds of the neem tree and which inhibits feeding of locusts and many other insects (Table 1) (Schmutterer, 1990; Sharma et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Responses to SOA conferred by Gr22b in I-a sensilla increased above 0.1 mM and appeared to saturate at 20 spikes/s.
source: Responses conferred by Gr22b increased above 0.1 mM and appeared to saturate at 20 spikes/s.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Neither parental control line responded to SOA at any concentration tested.
source: Neither of the parental control lines responded at any concentration.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: CUC, SOA, and AZA all elicit responses from wild type S-a sensilla, which express Gr22b endogenously.
source: We note that CUC, SOA, and AZA all elicit responses from wild type S-a sensilla, which express Gr22b endogenously.
evidence: This is an observation connecting the ectopic expression results to endogenous expression patterns.

claim: Gr58c conferred novel responses to MYR, STR, and COU in I-a sensilla.
source: Gr58c conferred novel responses to MYR, STR, and COU, and responses to QUI, LOB, and DEN that were greater than those of the control line (p<0.0001, except that for COU p<0.0005, and for MYR p<0.05, n≥16).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Gr58c conferred responses to QUI, LOB, and DEN that were greater than those of the control line in I-a sensilla.
source: Gr58c conferred novel responses to MYR, STR, and COU, and responses to QUI, LOB, and DEN that were greater than those of the control line (p<0.0001, except that for COU p<0.0005, and for MYR p<0.05, n≥16).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Gr58c is expressed in leg sensilla that respond to five of the six compounds tested.
source: We note that Gr58c is expressed in leg sensilla that respond to five of these compounds; the sixth was not tested in legs (Ling et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Gr2a and Gr10a conferred remarkably similar response profiles in I-a sensilla.
source: Remarkably similar response profiles were conferred by expression of Gr2a and Gr10a.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Both Gr2a and Gr10a conferred responses to caffeine (CAF), umbelliferone (UMB), and theophylline (TPH) in I-a sensilla.
source: Both receptors conferred responses to caffeine (CAF), umbelliferone (UMB), and theophylline (TPH), which elicit essentially no response from the control, and an increased response to LOB (p<0.0001, except p<0.01 for the TPH values and p<0.05 for CAF in the case of Gr10a, n≥8).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Gr2a and Gr10a are distantly related phylogenetically.
source: Despite this functional similarity, Gr2a and Gr10a are distantly related phylogenetically (Robertson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior phylogenetic analysis.

claim: CAF and TPH are present in coffee and tea and are closely related in structure.
source: CAF and TPH, which are present in coffee and tea, are closely related in structure; UMB is present in carrots and coriander and is structurally distinct (Table 1).
evidence: This is chemical knowledge presented in Table 1.

claim: UMB is present in carrots and coriander and is structurally distinct from CAF and TPH.
source: CAF and TPH, which are present in coffee and tea, are closely related in structure; UMB is present in carrots and coriander and is structurally distinct (Table 1).
evidence: This is chemical knowledge presented in Table 1.

claim: The response to UMB conferred by Gr2a in I-a sensilla increased above 0.3 mM and appeared to saturate at a level between 10 spikes/s and 15 spikes/s.
source: In an independent dose-response experiment, the response to UMB increased above 0.3 mM, and appeared to saturate at a level between 10 spikes/s and 15 spikes/s (Figure 3b; limited solubility of UMB precluded testing at higher concentrations).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Neither parental control responded to any tested concentration of UMB.
source: Neither parental control responded to any tested concentration of UMB.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Saturation of the response to UMB conferred by Gr2a was lower than that for the response to SOA conferred by Gr22b.
source: We note that saturation of the response to UMB conferred by Gr2a was lower than that for the response to SOA conferred by Gr22b (Figure 2c)
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figures 2c and 3b.

claim: The SOA response appeared to have a lower threshold and to saturate at a lower concentration than the response to UMB.
source: the SOA response also appeared to have a lower threshold and to saturate at a lower concentration than the response to UMB.
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figures 2c and 3b.

claim: Expression of Gr28b.a in I-a sensilla produced a modest response to MYR that was not observed in the control line.
source: When Gr28b.a was expressed, we observed a modest response to MYR that was not observed in the control line (p<0.05, n≥26), as well as an increased response to LOB (p<0.0001, n≥26).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Expression of Gr28b.a in I-a sensilla produced an increased response to LOB.
source: When Gr28b.a was expressed, we observed a modest response to MYR that was not observed in the control line (p<0.05, n≥26), as well as an increased response to LOB (p<0.0001, n≥26).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Expression of Gr28a in I-a sensilla produced an increase in response to LOB.
source: Gr28a produced an increase in response to LOB (p<0.0001, n≥24).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Expression of Gr36a in I-a sensilla produced no changes in the response profile.
source: Gr36a produced no changes in the response profile of I-a.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Gr36a could require a co-factor not present in I-a, or could function in response to a tastant not included in the panel.
source: Gr36a could require a co-factor not present in I-a, or could function in response to a tastant not included in the panel.
evidence: This is speculation about why Gr36a showed no effects.

claim: Expression of Gr28b.a in I-b sensilla conferred an increased response to aristolochic acid (ARI).
source: Expression of Gr28b.a in I-b sensilla, where it is expressed endogenously, conferred an increased response to aristolochic acid (ARI), as well as to berberine (BER) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Expression of Gr28b.a in I-b sensilla conferred an increased response to berberine (BER).
source: Expression of Gr28b.a in I-b sensilla, where it is expressed endogenously, conferred an increased response to aristolochic acid (ARI), as well as to berberine (BER) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Gr28b.a is expressed endogenously in I-b sensilla.
source: Expression of Gr28b.a in I-b sensilla, where it is expressed endogenously, conferred an increased response to aristolochic acid (ARI), as well as to berberine (BER) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on expression analysis from Weiss et al., 2011.

claim: Responses to ARI in I-b sensilla of the Gr89a-GAL4; UAS-Gr28b.a line were greater than in either parental control at the two higher concentrations tested.
source: The increase to ARI was confirmed in an independent dose-response analysis: responses in I-b sensilla of the Gr89a-GAL4; UAS-Gr28b.a line were greater than in either parental control at the two higher concentrations tested (Figure 4b; higher concentrations were not tested due to limited solubility).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: At the highest concentration of ARI tested, the response of Gr89a-GAL4; UAS-Gr28b.a approached 25 spikes/s.
source: At the highest concentration, the response of Gr89a-GAL4; UAS-Gr28b.a approached 25 spikes/s.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Expression of Gr28a in I-b sensilla conferred a novel response to saponin (SAP) not observed in the GAL4 control line.
source: Expression of Gr28a in I-b sensilla conferred a novel response to saponin (SAP) not observed in the GAL4 control line (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The novel response to SAP conferred by Gr28a was not observed in the UAS-Gr28a parental control.
source: the response was not observed in the UAS-Gr28a parental control either (1 spike/s ± 1, n=11).
evidence: This is supported by data from the UAS-Gr28a control.

claim: The production of a novel response to SAP by Gr28a expression in I-b sensilla was surprising, since Gr28a is expressed endogenously in I-b sensilla.
source: The production of this novel response was surprising, since Gr28a is expressed endogenously in I-b sensilla.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the surprising nature of the finding.

claim: Expression of Gr36a in I-b sensilla conferred no response.
source: Gr36a conferred no response to I-b, as in I-a.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The effects of expression of Gr28b.a and Gr28a in I-b differ from those in I-a.
source: Thus the effects of expression of Gr28b.a and Gr28a in I-b differ from those in I-a.
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figures 3a and 4a.

claim: No responses to ARI or SAP were conferred by expression of Gr28b.a or Gr28a, respectively, in I-a sensilla.
source: In contrast to I-b, no responses to ARI or SAP were conferred by expression of Gr28b.a or Gr28a, respectively, in I-a sensilla.
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figures 3a and 4a.

claim: The increases in response to MYR and LOB observed in I-a were not observed in I-b.
source: Conversely, the increases in response to MYR and LOB that were observed in I-a were not observed in I-b.
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figures 3a and 4a.

claim: Some Grs have distinct functions in different neuronal contexts.
source: The simplest interpretation of these results, taken together, is that some Grs have distinct functions in different neuronal contexts.
evidence: This is an interpretation inferred from the comparative data.

claim: No increases in response were observed to any tastant with any receptor when expressed in S-a sensilla.
source: We also expressed the three Grs in S-a sensilla. No increases in response were observed to any tastant, with any receptor.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Expression of UAS-Gr28a in S-a sensilla produced responses to DEN, UMB, ARI, and BER that were lower than in the parental control line.
source: However, a striking effect was observed in the response to DEN, UMB, ARI, and BER upon expression of UAS-Gr28a in S-a: responses were lower than in the parental control line (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Expression of Gr22b in S-a sensilla conferred an increased response to SOA and CUC.
source: We first tested the effects of Gr22b expression in S-a sensilla. As in I-a, Gr22b expression conferred an increased response to SOA and CUC (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The Gr89a-GAL4; UAS-Gr22b line responded strongly to AZA in S-a sensilla, but the responses of the control lines were equally strong.
source: The Gr89a-GAL4; UAS-Gr22b line also responded strongly to AZA, as in I-a, but the responses of the control lines were equally strong.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Expression of Gr22b in S-a sensilla produced dramatic reductions in the responses to a number of tastants, such as DEN.
source: Dramatic reductions, however, were produced by Gr22b expression in the responses of S-a to a number of tastants, such as DEN (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The decreased DEN response in S-a produced by Gr22b expression is in contrast to the increased DEN response in I-a produced by expression of the same receptor.
source: This decreased DEN response in S-a is in contrast to the increased DEN response in I-a produced by expression of the same receptor (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figures 3a and 5a.

claim: Suppression of response by Gr22b is observed in a cell that has been engineered to overexpress one of its endogenous receptors.
source: This suppression is particularly interesting because Gr22b is expressed endogenously in S-a sensilla; thus suppression of response is observed in a cell that has been engineered to overexpress one of its endogenous receptors.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the suppression finding to the endogenous expression pattern.

claim: Gr58c suppressed the responses of S-a sensilla to UMB and ARI.
source: Gr58c also suppressed the responses of S-a sensilla, in this case to UMB and ARI (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Gr58c did not suppress the response to DEN in S-a sensilla.
source: Gr58c did not suppress the response to DEN; thus Gr58c and Gr22b both suppress responses to bitter compounds, but different compounds.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Gr58c and Gr22b both suppress responses to bitter compounds, but different compounds.
source: Gr58c did not suppress the response to DEN; thus Gr58c and Gr22b both suppress responses to bitter compounds, but different compounds.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the suppression patterns of Gr58c and Gr22b.

claim: Gr2a reduced responses in S-a to several tastants, including DEN, SPS, STR, and LOB.
source: Gr2a reduced responses in S-a to several tastants, including DEN, SPS, STR, and LOB.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Gr10a showed suppressive effects in S-a sensilla.
source: Gr10a also showed suppressive effects in S-a.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The profiles produced by Gr2a and Gr10a in S-a sensilla were very similar to each other.
source: Moreover, the profiles produced by Gr2a and Gr10a were very similar to each other (Figure 5b), as in I-a (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5b and 3a.

claim: At all concentrations tested, responses to SPS were lower in the line expressing Gr2a than in the parental control lines.
source: At all concentrations tested, responses to SPS were lower in the line expressing Gr2a than in the parental control lines.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Suppression of SPS response by Gr22b was observed at both 3 mM and 10 mM concentrations.
source: Suppression of SPS response by Gr22b was observed at both 3 mM and 10 mM concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Suppression of responses was observed not only in S-a sensilla but also in I-b sensilla.
source: Suppression of responses was observed not only in S-a sensilla but also in I-b sensilla (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Expression of Gr22b in I-b sensilla conferred novel responses to SOA, CUC and AZA.
source: Although Gr22b expression conferred novel responses to SOA, CUC and AZA, as it did in I-a sensilla (Figure 3a), it suppressed the responses to THE, CAF, TPH, and UMB.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Expression of Gr22b in I-b sensilla suppressed the responses to THE, CAF, TPH, and UMB.
source: Although Gr22b expression conferred novel responses to SOA, CUC and AZA, as it did in I-a sensilla (Figure 3a), it suppressed the responses to THE, CAF, TPH, and UMB.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The ability of Gr22b to confer entirely novel responses and suppress endogenous ones in I-b sensilla is especially surprising given that Gr22b is endogenously expressed in I-b bitter neurons.
source: The ability of Gr22b to confer entirely novel responses and suppress endogenous ones in I-b sensilla is especially surprising given that Gr22b is endogenously expressed in I-b bitter neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the surprising nature of the finding.

claim: Expression of Gr58c in I-b sensilla showed reduced responses to CAF, TPH, and UMB.
source: Likewise, Gr58c showed reduced responses to CAF, TPH, and UMB, while conferring response to DEN and LOB, two compounds to which Gr58c expression also confers responses in I-a sensilla (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Expression of Gr58c in I-b sensilla conferred response to DEN and LOB.
source: Likewise, Gr58c showed reduced responses to CAF, TPH, and UMB, while conferring response to DEN and LOB, two compounds to which Gr58c expression also confers responses in I-a sensilla (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Gr2a and Gr10a behaved similarly in I-b sensilla, in that their expression had no effects.
source: Gr2a and Gr10a again behaved similarly in I-b sensilla, in that their expression had no effects.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The lack of effect of Gr2a and Gr10a in I-b sensilla is in contrast to their conferral of responses in I-a sensilla and their suppression of responses in S-a sensilla.
source: Their lack of effect in I-b sensilla is in contrast to their conferral of responses in I-a sensilla and their suppression of responses in S-a sensilla.
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figures 3a, 5b, and 5d.

claim: Suppression occurred broadly: in both S-a and I-b, by several different receptors, and with several different tastants.
source: In summary, suppression occurred broadly: in both S-a and I-b, by several different receptors, and with several different tastants.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Expression of an individual receptor in a given sensillum increased the responses to some tastants and decreased the responses to others.
source: Expression of an individual receptor in a given sensillum increased the responses to some tastants and decreased the responses to others (e.g. Gr22b; CUC and DEN in S-a).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the data, with Gr22b in S-a as an example.

claim: Expression of an individual receptor increased the response to a tastant in one sensillum type and decreased it in another.
source: Expression of an individual receptor increased the response to a tastant in one sensillum type and decreased it in another (e.g. Gr22b; DEN in I-a and S-a).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the data, with Gr22b and DEN as an example.

claim: Suppression was observed both in cases of overexpression and ectopic expression.
source: Suppression was observed both in cases of overexpression and ectopic expression, i.e. expression of a receptor in a neuron that either does (e.g. Gr22b in S-a) or does not (e.g. Gr2a in S-a) express it endogenously in wild type.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the data.

claim: In some sensilla a receptor produced decreased responses but no increased responses.
source: Finally, in some sensilla a receptor produced decreased responses but no increased responses (e.g. Gr2a in S-a).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the data, with Gr2a in S-a as an example.

claim: Gr59c is the sole receptor in the I-a bitter neurons other than the commonly expressed receptors (CERs).
source: We next considered Gr59c, which is the sole receptor in the I-a bitter neurons other than the commonly expressed receptors (CERs) (Figure 1)
evidence: This is based on expression analysis shown in Figure 1 and from Weiss et al., 2011.

claim: Gr59c is expressed in S-a but not I-b.
source: it is also expressed in S-a but not I-b.
evidence: This is based on expression analysis from Weiss et al., 2011 and Figure 1.

claim: A previous test with a limited number of tastants found that misexpression of Gr59c increased or decreased the responses to certain tastants.
source: A previous test with a limited number of tastants found that misexpression of Gr59c increased or decreased the responses to certain tastants (Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Expression of Gr59c increased responses to LOB, DEN and BER in all three sensillum types (I-b, S-a, and I-a).
source: Using our complete panel of 21 tastants we confirmed and extended these results: we found that expression of Gr59c increased responses to LOB, DEN and BER in all three sensillum types, and suppressed many of the larger responses in I-b and S-a (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Expression of Gr59c suppressed many of the larger responses in I-b and S-a.
source: Using our complete panel of 21 tastants we confirmed and extended these results: we found that expression of Gr59c increased responses to LOB, DEN and BER in all three sensillum types, and suppressed many of the larger responses in I-b and S-a (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The net result of Gr59c expression in each sensillum type was a profile in which LOB, DEN, and BER elicited the strongest responses.
source: Interestingly, the net result in each sensillum type was a profile in which LOB, DEN, and BER elicited the strongest responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Deletion of Gr59c eliminated the responses to LOB, DEN, and BER in I-a sensilla.
source: As expected, deletion of Gr59c eliminated the responses to LOB, DEN, and BER (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: ΔGr59c I-a sensilla showed strong novel responses to THE, CAF, UMB, and TPH.
source: However, contrary to our expectations, △Gr59c I-a sensilla showed strong novel responses to THE, CAF, UMB, and TPH.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The response profile of the mutant I-a sensillum is similar to that of control I-b sensilla.
source: Intriguingly, the response profile of the mutant I-a sensillum is similar to that of control I-b sensilla (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a comparison of data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Expression of a UAS-Gr59c construct in ΔGr59c flies was sufficient to restore a profile similar to that of wild-type I-a sensilla.
source: Expression of a UAS-Gr59c construct in △Gr59c flies was sufficient to restore a profile similar to that of wild-type I-a sensilla, providing evidence that the mutant phenotype is in fact due to loss of Gr59c.
evidence: This is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The rescue of the ΔGr59c phenotype argues against the notion that the flanking Gr59d gene contributes to the ΔGr59c phenotype.
source: We note that this rescue argues against the notion that the flanking Gr59d gene, which is also removed by the Gr59c deletion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), contributes to the △Gr59c phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference from the rescue experiment.

claim: A GAL4-Gr59d driver shows expression in S-a bitter taste neurons but not in I-a sensilla.
source: Moreover, a GAL4-Gr59d driver shows expression in S-a bitter taste neurons but not in I-a sensilla, consistent with the interpretation that the △Gr59c phenotype observed in I-a sensilla arises from loss of Gr59c alone (Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior expression analysis.

claim: ΔGr59c has no strong effect on the S-a bitter neuron, other than a decrease in the response to DEN.
source: We asked whether △Gr59c has a similar effect on the S-a bitter neuron, which also expresses Gr59c. We found no effect, other than a decrease in the response to DEN (Figure 7—figure supplement 2, p<0.0001, n≥12).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lack of a strong mutant phenotype in S-a may reflect the much greater molecular complexity of S-a compared to I-a.
source: The lack of a strong mutant phenotype may reflect the much greater molecular complexity of S-a: apart from the CERs, the S-a bitter neuron expresses 24 Grs, whereas its I-a counterpart expresses only Gr59c.
evidence: This is speculation about why the phenotype differs between S-a and I-a.

claim: The difference between the ΔGr59c phenotype in S-a and I-a sensilla provides a further example of how the function of a bitter Gr may differ in different neuronal contexts.
source: The difference between the △Gr59c phenotype in the two sensilla provides a further example of how the function of a bitter Gr may differ in different neuronal contexts.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the ΔGr59c phenotypes in different sensilla.

claim: Expression of Gr59c-GAL4 appeared the same in the ΔGr59c labellum as in the control.
source: If the I-a bitter neurons underwent a complete change in cell fate to that of I-b bitter neurons, then one would expect these neurons to lose expression of Gr59c-GAL4. This outcome was not observed (Figure 8, top two panels). In fact, expression of Gr59c-GAL4 appeared the same in the △Gr59c labellum as in the control.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8.

claim: None of the three drivers that are expressed in I-b (Gr28a-, Gr28b.a- and Gr22b-GAL4) were expressed in ΔGr59c I-a sensilla.
source: Likewise, none of the three drivers that are expressed in I-b were expressed in △Gr59c I-a sensilla (Figure 8, bottom six panels).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The imaging results argue against the hypothesis that I-a sensilla undergo a complete fate change switch to I-b sensilla.
source: These results argue against the hypothesis that I-a sensilla undergo a complete fate change switch to I-b sensilla.
evidence: This is an inference from the imaging data in Figure 8.

claim: When the temperature was not increased at all and repression of UAS-Gr59c was continuous, a ΔGr59c phenotype was observed.
source: When the temperature was not increased at all and repression of UAS-Gr59c was continuous, a △Gr59c phenotype was observed, as expected, demonstrating that GAL80ts successfully suppressed UAS-Gr59c expression at low temperature (blue bar in Figure 9c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: If the temperature was increased either during pupal development, at 1d after eclosion, or at 5d after eclosion, a wild-type I-a phenotype was restored in every case.
source: However, if the temperature was increased either during pupal development, at 1d after eclosion, or at 5d after eclosion, a wild-type I-a phenotype was restored in every case.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: Rescue by the UAS-Gr59c transgene could occur even after eclosion, in a mature fly.
source: Thus, rescue by the UAS-Gr59c transgene could occur even after eclosion, in a mature fly.
evidence: This is an inference from the temporal rescue data in Figure 9.

claim: The temporal rescue results argue against a developmental requirement for Gr59c.
source: These results argue against a developmental requirement for Gr59c.
evidence: This is an inference from the temporal rescue data in Figure 9.

claim: The temporal rescue results are consistent with a physiological role for Gr59c in determining the response profile of the sensillum.
source: Rather, they are consistent with a physiological role for Gr59c in determining the response profile of the sensillum.
evidence: This is an inference from the temporal rescue data in Figure 9.

claim: Expression of Gr28a in ΔGr59c I-a sensilla conferred response to eight tastants.
source: Expression of Gr28a in △Gr59c I-a sensilla conferred response to eight tastants (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Expression of Gr28a in wild type I-a sensilla increased responses to none of the eight tastants to which it conferred responses in ΔGr59c I-a sensilla.
source: By contrast, expression of Gr28a in wild type I-a sensilla increased responses to none of these tastants (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figures 10 and 3a.

claim: Expression of Gr36a in ΔGr59c I-a sensilla conferred responses to 6 tastants, while suppressing responses to two.
source: Expression of Gr36a in △Gr59c I-a sensilla conferred responses to 6 tastants, while suppressing responses to two.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Expression of Gr36a conferred no changes in response profiles of wild type I-a, S-a, or I-b sensilla.
source: By contrast, expression of Gr36a conferred no changes in response profiles of wild type I-a sensilla (Figure 3a), or S-a or I-b sensilla (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is a comparison of data from Figures 10, 3a, and 4.

claim: Expression of Gr28b.a in ΔGr59c I-a sensilla conferred an increased response to ARI.
source: Expression of Gr28b.a conferred an increased response to ARI, which is consistent with the increased response to ARI found in I-b sensilla (Figure 4a,b; MYR was not tested).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Expression of Gr22b in ΔGr59c I-a sensilla conferred responses to SOA and AZA.
source: Gr22b had conferred strong, novel responses to CUC, SOA and AZA in I-a (Figure 3a), and we wanted to determine if in the absence of Gr59c these responses were still conferred. We tested two of these responses, SOA and AZA, and both were conserved (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Expression of Gr22b in ΔGr59c I-a sensilla conferred responses to ESC and SPS.
source: Responses were also conferred to ESC and SPS, and several responses were suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Expression of Gr22b in ΔGr59c I-a sensilla suppressed several responses.
source: Responses were also conferred to ESC and SPS, and several responses were suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Removal of Gr59c from I-a sensilla allowed Grs to confer novel responses that were not observed in the presence of Gr59c.
source: In summary, removal of Gr59c from I-a sensilla allowed Grs to confer novel responses that were not observed in the presence of Gr59c.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the data in Figure 10.

claim: The results are consistent with the notion that Grs may interact with each other or compete for common co-factors.
source: The results are also consistent with the notion that Grs may interact with each other or compete for common co-factors.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: All expressed Grs had functional effects in at least one neuronal type.
source:
All of our studies have been carried out in vivo, in a natural laboratory: in taste neurons in gustatory sensilla of the labellum, which have evolved over the course of hundreds of millions of years to sample, detect, and signal taste information. The taste stimuli have been delivered by direct contact in a manner that simulates natural sampling of tastants, and the responses have been measured by recording action potentials, the signals transmitted to the brain.

All expressed Grs had functional effects in at least one neuronal type.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings across all tested Grs.

claim: The tested Grs are dispersed widely across tissues, developmental time, and the phylogenetic tree of Grs.
source: Moreover, the tested receptors are dispersed widely not only across tissues and developmental time, but also across the phylogenetic tree of Grs (Robertson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on the expression patterns shown in Table 2 and phylogenetic analysis from Robertson et al., 2003.

claim: The profiles of Gr2a and Gr10a were very similar in each of three sensillum types examined.
source: There was one notable exception, however: the profiles of Gr2a and Gr10a were very similar in each of three sensillum types examined (Figures 3, 5b,d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Gr2a and Gr10a are on distant branches of the Gr phylogenetic tree.
source: Gr2a and Gr10a are not recently duplicated genes, but rather are on distant branches of the Gr phylogenetic tree (Robertson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Similar odor response spectra are conferred by the D. melanogaster and D. pseudoobscura orthologs of Or71a, which contain only 59% amino acid sequence identity.
source: We have previously found that similar odor response spectra are conferred by the D. melanogaster and D. pseudoobscura orthologs of Or71a, which contain only 59% amino acid sequence identity (Ray et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Gr2a and Gr10a exhibit only 32% amino acid sequence identity.
source: Gr2a and Gr10a provide an even more extreme case: they exhibit only 32% identity.
evidence: This is a statement about sequence similarity.

claim: Bitter taste neurons are heterogeneous.
source: A key finding of this study is that expression of individual Grs produced different effects in different bitter taste neurons (Figure 11, Figure 11—figure supplement 1). This finding supports an emerging theme in the field of taste: that bitter taste neurons are heterogeneous (Weiss et al., 2011; Meunier et al., 2003; French et al., 2015; Glendinning et al., 2006; Glendinning et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the findings of this study and citations to prior research.

claim: A long-held concept in the field has been that all bitter taste neurons are identical and function identically to warn the animal indiscriminately of toxic compounds.
source: Historically, a long-held concept in the field has been that all bitter taste neurons are identical, and that they function identically to warn the animal indiscriminately of toxic compounds (Freeman and Dahanukar, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about historical views in the field, supported by citation.

claim: An emerging concept is that bitter taste neurons are distinguishable, both in terms of response profile and receptor expression.
source: An emerging concept is that bitter taste neurons are distinguishable, both in terms of response profile and receptor expression (Weiss et al., 2011; Ling et al., 2014; Meunier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: The differing effects of expressing an individual Gr in varying neuronal contexts adds evidence to support the view that different bitter taste neurons are functionally distinct.
source: The differing effects of expressing an individual Gr in varying neuronal contexts adds another line of evidence to support the view that different bitter taste neurons are functionally distinct, thereby endowing the system with richer coding capacity.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings of this study.

claim: Expression of Grs produced three kinds of effects: a novel response, an increased response, and a decreased response.
source: Expression of Grs produced three kinds of effects: a novel response to a particular tastant, not observed in either parental control; an increased response to a tastant, greater than that observed in controls; a decreased response to a tastant, i.e. suppression.
evidence: This is a summary of the types of effects observed in the study.

claim: All three kinds of effects (novel, increased, and decreased responses) were observed broadly, and most receptors exhibited all three kinds of effects.
source: All three effects were observed broadly, and most receptors exhibited all three kinds of effects (Figure 11, Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings shown in Figure 11.

claim: Different receptors conferred varying effects in different neurons or in response to different tastants.
source: However, there was specificity to the effects, in that different receptors conferred varying effects in different neurons or in response to different tastants.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the data.

claim: Expression of single bitter Grs in sugar-sensitive neurons or heterologous expression systems has not yielded bitter responses.
source: The possibility of interactions among bitter Grs, and in particular the formation of Gr heteromers, is consistent with the results of several previous studies. First, expression of single bitter Grs in sugar-sensitive neurons or heterologous expression systems has not yielded bitter responses, consistent with the possibility that a combination of bitter Grs is required (Liman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The responses to some bitter compounds were reduced by mutation of any of multiple Grs.
source: Second, the responses to some bitter compounds were reduced by mutation of any of multiple Grs, consistent with the notion that these Grs combine to form a functional multimer (Lee et al., 2009; 2010; 2012; Moon et al., 2006; 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the antenna, two Grs, Gr21a and Gr63a, are coexpressed and together confer response to carbon dioxide.
source: In the antenna, two Grs, Gr21a and Gr63a, are coexpressed and together confer response to carbon dioxide (Jones et al., 2007; Kwon et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is evidence for subunit interactions among sugar receptors.
source: There is evidence for subunit interactions among sugar receptors (Fujii et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Responses conferred by expression of individual sugar receptor genes in an antennal neuron agree well with the responses lost by mutations of the same individual Gr genes.
source: although elegant experiments have shown that responses conferred by expression of individual sugar receptor genes in an antennal neuron agree well with the responses lost by mutations of the same individual Gr genes (Freeman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Changes in the expression of a taste receptor can generate increased responses, decreased responses, and novel responses.
source: Our results suggest a rich, alternative means of generating variation in chemosensory signaling. We have found that changes in the expression of a taste receptor can generate a wide variety of effects: increased responses, decreased responses, and novel responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings and their implications.

claim: Simple alterations in regulatory sequences that govern the cellular specificity of expression, or the level of expression, could change the response specificities of taste neurons in dramatic and beneficial ways.
source: Accordingly, simple alterations in regulatory sequences that govern the cellular specificity of expression, or the level of expression, could change the response specificities of taste neurons in dramatic and beneficial ways.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary implications based on the findings.

claim: The organization of the taste system featuring the coexpression of many Grs in individual neurons may provide numerous degrees of freedom for altering the response patterns of the neurons.
source: Thus, the organization of the taste system—featuring the coexpression of many Grs in individual neurons—may provide numerous degrees of freedom for altering the response patterns of the neurons, via either the gain or loss of receptor function.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the taste system organization.

claim: A network of coexpressed Grs, sensitive to relative levels of expression, could provide a means of modulating taste sensitivity in response to short-term changes in either the environment or the internal state of the fly.
source: A network of coexpressed Grs, sensitive to relative levels of expression, could also provide a means of modulating taste sensitivity in response to short-term changes in either the environment or the internal state of the fly.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Alterations in the expression of Gr59c in the mature fly induced changes in taste sensitivity.
source: We found that alterations in the expression of Gr59c in the mature fly induced changes in taste sensitivity (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Short-term changes in Gr transcription or post-transcriptional processing could be a mechanism of altering taste response to meet the short-term needs of a hungry or satiated fly.
source: Thus, short-term changes in Gr transcription or post-transcriptional processing could in principle be a mechanism of altering taste response to meet the short-term needs of a hungry or satiated fly (Prestia et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about mechanisms of taste modulation, supported by citations.

claim: The functional organization of the taste system differs from that of the olfactory system in that the 60 Gr genes are more highly coexpressed in a smaller number of neuronal types than the 60 Or genes.
source: In a more general sense, the functional organization of the taste system differs from that of the olfactory system in that the 60 Gr genes are more highly coexpressed in a smaller number of neuronal types than the 60 Or genes.
evidence: This is a comparison of organizational principles between taste and olfactory systems.

claim: The pattern of organization of the taste system may entail some loss of discriminatory power, but could provide a degree of evolutionary and regulatory flexibility.
source: This pattern of organization may in principle entail some loss of discriminatory power, but it could provide a degree of evolutionary and regulatory flexibility that may serve the needs of the animal well.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional trade-offs of taste system organization.

claim: Most Ors are believed to bind odorants.
source: For example, Grs might compete for binding to a common co-factor. In the olfactory system, most ORNs express one of ~60 Ors that are believed to bind odorants, along with a common co-receptor, Orco, which is required for function of the Or (Larsson et al., 2004; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the olfactory system, supported by citations.

claim: Orco is a common co-receptor required for function of the Or.
source: In the olfactory system, most ORNs express one of ~60 Ors that are believed to bind odorants, along with a common co-receptor, Orco, which is required for function of the Or (Larsson et al., 2004; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the olfactory system, supported by citations.

claim: An RNA-Seq analysis was consistent with a 1:1 stoichiometry of Ors and Orco in the antenna.
source: Moreover, an RNA-Seq analysis was consistent with a 1:1 stoichiometry of Ors and Orco in the antenna (Menuz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Ors can confer inhibitory as well as excitatory responses to olfactory receptor neurons.
source: We note that Ors can confer inhibitory as well as excitatory responses to olfactory receptor neurons (Hallem et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.
